podcast.title: Film Career – Vehicle for New Music
podcast.body: Elvis Presley starred in a series of movies, often described as "terrible," which primarily served as vehicles for him to release new music. This trend followed the initial integration of rock and roll into films in the 1950s. "Then along came Elvis with his string of terrible movies, all of which were used as vehicles for new music."

podcast.title: Film Company Interference in Music
podcast.body: For his first film, Elvis was annoyed that songs were added to the script, and his regular band (Scotty Moore, Bill Black, DJ Fontana) was not allowed to play on the soundtrack. They were replaced by Hollywood session musicians whom the film company believed could "sound hillbilly enough." "he found out to his annoyance that he wasn't allowed to use Scotty Bill and DJ on the soundtrack, because the film company didn't think they could sound hillbilly enough."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Film Quality Comparison
podcast.body: Elvis's films were considered "masterpieces of the cinema" when compared to the numerous exploitation films starring popular DJs of the era, which typically featured interchangeable plots about kids wanting to put on a dance. "They were the kind of thing that made Elvis's films look like masterpieces of the cinema and tended to involve a bunch of kids who wanted to put on a dance at their local school, or similar interchangeable plots."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Film Songs as Contextual Storytelling (General)
podcast.body: Many songs Elvis recorded for his films, especially in later years (e.g., "There's No Room to Rumba in a Sports Car," "Yoga Is as Yoga Does," "Queenie Wahini's Papaya," "Ito Eats"), are often criticized as terrible when heard in isolation. This is because they were primarily intended to function within the film's narrative, serving as part of the storytelling rather than as standalone musical compositions. "But in part, that's because they are not intended to work as songs divorced from their context in the film."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Film Studio MGM Connection
podcast.body: MGM, a prominent film studio, successfully signed Elvis Presley for movie roles, indicating his crossover appeal beyond music. "MGM, the film studio, the third signed Elvis up so successfully."

podcast.title: First Album Material Selection
podcast.body: For his first album, Elvis mostly recorded R&B and Rockabilly covers, and almost all of this material was chosen by him, contrasting with later sessions where material was imposed. "Almost all of these were Elvis's own choice of material."

podcast.body: Lee Denson taught Elvis his first guitar chords, the same person who instructed Dorsey Burnette. "Lee Denson, who had taught both Dorsey and Elvis their first guitar courts."

podcast.title: First Meeting with Burnettes
podcast.body: Roy Orbison met the Burnette brothers during a chance encounter in a Memphis radio station while waiting for a lift with Elvis Presley; the Burnettes were found inside the lift in the middle of a fist fight. "The first time Roy Orbison met them he was standing in a Memphis radio station chatting with Elbas Presley and waiting for a lift."

podcast.title: First True Rock and Roll Star
podcast.body: Elvis Presley, a young white truck driver who was said to sound like he was black, became the first true rock and roll star. In the context of the 1950s, if rock and roll was considered alternative to the mainstream, then Elvis could be seen as the first alternative music star. "Elvis Presley was the first true rocket roll star, and if rocket roll was the alternative to the mainstream in the 1950s, we could also say that Elvis was our first alternative music star too."

podcast.title: Formal "Below the Waist" Ban (2nd & 3rd Ed Sullivan Shows)
podcast.body: By Elvis Presley's second and, subsequently, third appearances on The Ed Sullivan Show, a strict directive was in place: it was "literally prohibited" to film him from the waist down for the entire duration of the program. This official ban underscored the controversy surrounding his movements. "Ya en este segundo programa, incluso en el tercer programa que haría con el sul-bank, ya estaba literalmente prohibido enfocarlo de cintura para abajo durante todo el programa."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Foundational Rock Duo
podcast.body: Alongside Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley is credited with providing the initial one-two punch that established the foundations of rock and roll, setting the genre on its path. "Not one two-punch of Elvis and Chuck started us on the road to where we are today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Genius of Elvis
podcast.body: Elvis is emphatically described as a "genius," acknowledging his profound impact and undeniable talent in music. "El Viseron genio, es que escucha el Viseron puñete lo genio."

podcast.title: Graceland Post-Army Return
podcast.body: Elvis had only a couple of weeks to settle into Graceland, the home he bought for his mother but barely inhabited before his draft. Upon his return, it was to be shared with his father and his father's new, much younger girlfriend, whom Elvis "definitely did not approve." "He had a couple of weeks to settle in at Graceland, the home he had bought for his mother."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Grave Visit
podcast.body: Importantly, during his two-week post-army leave, Elvis visited his mother's grave for the first time, a deeply personal moment for him. "And most importantly to him, he visited the grave of his mother for the first time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Hatred of Fish – Fish Banned from Graceland
podcast.body: Elvis Presley hated fish so intensely because of its smell that he banned it entirely from Graceland. "Hated fish so much for its smell that he banned it from Graceland."

podcast.title: Historically Top-Selling Artist
podcast.body: Elvis Presley is ranked among the highest-selling artists in history. Record labels estimate his sales to be between 500 and 600 million copies. However, independent sales analysis organizations place his sales figures more precisely around 200 to 215 million copies.

podcast.title: Immediate Reissue by RCA
podcast.body: After signing Elvis, RCA Records quickly reissued his Sun singles, "I forgot to remember to forget" and "Mystery Train," while waiting for his first recording session with the new label. "RCA quickly reissued, I forgot to remember to forget, and mystery train, while they were waiting for Elvis's first recording session for his new label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Impact of Loose Pants
podcast.body: Elvis Presley frequently wore "loose, very fluid pants." When he moved and danced, these garments caused his entire crotch area to become highly accentuated, contributing to the perceived explicitness of his performance. "El vis llevaba pantalones flojos muy fluidos, entonces al moverse así, pues toda la entrepierna se le marcaba mucho."

podcast.title: Impact of Success on Sun Records
podcast.body: Elvis's success created a significant problem for Sun Records, an independent label, due to cash flow issues. The demand for hundreds of thousands of copies meant paying pressing plants upfront while distributors paid months later, if at all. "Something is more deadly to the indie label than a hit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Impact on Rock's Momentum
podcast.body: Elvis is cited as one of the key figures whose emergence, alongside Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis, made rock music unstoppable. Despite widespread criticism, record burnings, and attempts by authorities to crack down on the genre, rock solidified its presence in music following his rise. "None of this actually slowed anything down, of course. We got Elvis, then Little Richard, then Jerry Lee Lewis. And then after that, the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Incorporation of "I Got a Woman" into Repertoire
podcast.body: Elvis Presley, a musician noted for having "church music in his veins," quickly integrated Ray Charles's "I Got a Woman" into his stage repertoire, helping to establish it as a rock and roll standard. "I got a woman went to number one on the R&B chart and quickly entered the stage repertoire of another musician who had church music in his veins."

podcast.title: Influence on British Rock
podcast.body: While British commercial rock and roll lagged, British teenagers were actively listening to Elvis's American records. Harry Webb (later Cliff Richard) became deeply obsessed with Elvis at 16, striving to emulate his appearance, vocal style, and stage movements. Tommy Steele also achieved a number one hit by copying Elvis's vocal mannerisms. "British teenagers were instead listening to American records by Buddy Holly or Little Richard, the Avley Brothers or Elvis, none of whose recordings had anything to do with anything that was being made by the British commercial rock and roll industry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence on Johnny Cash's Career Path
podcast.body: Johnny Cash followed the exact same career path as Elvis Presley, being managed by Elvis's first proper manager Bob Neal and performing on the Louisiana Hayride, a country music radio show where Elvis built his reputation. "He was following the exact same career path as Elvis Presley."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence on The Black Keys
podcast.body: Elvis was one of the favorite artists that inspired the short hooks used in the composition of songs for The Black Keys' *El Camino* album, indicating a classic rock and roll influence. "and Elvis".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Catching Up With The Black Keys

podcast.title: Influence on Videoclips
podcast.body: Films starring Elvis Presley, along with those of The Beatles, established many of the early standards for videoclips, such as camera plane changes synchronized with the music's rhythm or the inclusion of short narrative segments during performances. "Las películas de Elvis o las de los Beatles se sentaron muchas de los estándares del videoclip."

podcast.title: Influenced by Wynonie Harris's Stage Presence
podcast.body: Many observers who discussed Elvis Presley's performances in later years commented that his distinctive stage acts, including his hip thrusts and leg shaking, were merely a "watered down version" of what Wynonie Harris had been doing earlier in his career. "Lots of people who spoke about Elvis Presley in later years said that his performances, hip thrusts and leg shaking at all were just a watered down version of what Wainoni Harris had been doing."

podcast.title: Initial Career Ambition: Gospel Quartet
podcast.body: Elvis's earliest ambition, even before meeting Sam Phillips, was to be a member of a gospel quartet, as he loved to sing harmony. This foundational aspiration influenced his increasing use of backing vocalists throughout his career. "Elvis's first ambition, the aspiration he had right at the beginning of his career, was to be a member of a gospel quartet."

podcast.title: Initial Worry from Johnny Cash
podcast.body: When Johnny Cash saw Elvis perform on a flatbed truck, he was immediately worried that at 22, he was too old to achieve stardom compared to the clearly teenage Elvis. "Cash was immediately worried, Elvis was clearly a teenager, and Cash himself was a grown man of 22."

podcast.title: Insistence on The Jordanaires
podcast.body: After discovering that Steve Sholes had used only Gordon Stoker of The Jordanaires along with members of The Speer Family for backing vocals in initial RCA sessions as a cost-cutting measure, Elvis insisted that all members of The Jordanaires be employed for all his future sessions. "When Elvis found out at a later session that this had happened as a cost-cutting measure, he insisted that all the Jordanaires be employed at his future sessions."

podcast.title: John Lennon's Quote on Influence
podcast.body: John Lennon famously stated, "before Elvis there was nothing," reflecting the profound cultural impact Elvis Presley had, eclipsing all music prior to him. "lead John Lennon to say before Elvis there was nothing."

podcast.title: King of Rock and Roll Designation
podcast.body: Elvis Presley transitioned from a minor regional country star to "the King of Rock and Roll" and a "cultural phenomenon" upon signing with RCA Records and releasing his first major label single, "Heartbreak Hotel." podcast.title: Later Acquaintance, Not Close Friend
podcast.body: While he became friendly with the Burnettes later on, Elvis was consistently more of a "friend of friends" than an actual close friend, even when they were colleagues at Crown Electric. "Then while they became friendly later on, Elvis was always more of a friend of friends than he was an actual friend of theirs, even when he was a colleague of Dorsey's at Crown Electric."

podcast.title: Later Vocal Style Evolution
podcast.body: Although Elvis Presley's early singing was distinct from Gene Vincent's, his later material would increasingly incorporate the "hiccups and gasps" that Vincent used. At the time of "Be-Bop-A-Lula's" release, the differences in their vocal techniques would have been more immediately apparent to listeners. podcast.body: The pattern established in his early career indicated that whenever Elvis chose his own material and followed his instincts, the music was good. Conversely, when music was chosen for him by others, even sympathetic figures like Sam Phillips, the music suffered. "Whenever Elvis got to choose his own material and follow his own instincts, the results would be good music."

podcast.title: Memphis Charity Show Appearance

podcast.title: Uncontrollable Audience Reaction
podcast.body: Despite the post-production efforts to control the visual focus on Elvis Presley, the real challenge was managing the audience's reaction. Young women in the studio audience reportedly "went absolutely crazy" when Elvis began to sing, creating such "din, noise, and discontrol" that the program ultimately became a myth. "El problema era controlar la reacción del público. Al final Ed Zulligan estaba asesinado porque no se notase que todas las jóvenes que estaban en el programa de público se habían vuelto absolutamente locas cuando Elvis había empezado a cantar."

podcast.title: Urban Legend: The Bottle in Crotch
podcast.body: An urban legend claims that Elvis Presley intentionally placed a small bottle in his crotch to draw attention during his performances. However, this part of the story is "categorically denied" by others, leaving it as a contested piece of folklore. "una leyenda urbana que nos dice que Elvis había puesto una pequeña botella para llamar la atención."

podcast.title: Vocal Comparison with Gene Vincent
podcast.body: Many people noted the sonic and stylistic similarities between Elvis Presley's music and Gene Vincent's "Be-Bop-A-Lula." However, critics observed distinct differences in their vocal styles: Elvis was consistently "fully in control, playful and exuberant," whereas Vincent's performance was "tenser and twitchier" with a thinner voice. "While Elvis is fully in control at all times, playful and exuberant, Gene Vincent is tense and twitchy."

podcast.title: Vocal Expression Controversy
podcast.body: Elvis was one of several artists, including R&B acts, The Beatles, Dylan, Jagger, New Wavers, and rappers, whose vocal expressions were met with decades of criticism following the invention of the microphone. His singing style was seen by purists as a "degenerate form of singing," challenging older norms established before amplified vocals. "R&B acts, Elvis, The Beatles, Dylan, Jagger, New Waivers, rappers all the way up to and beyond death medillars."

xref.title: Robert Smith's "The Hair" and Controversial Haircut (Late 1986)
xref.body: As one of the biggest bands from the early 1980s Goth/Dark Stuff scene, The Cure's look, particularly Robert Smith's signature "The Hair"—a long, unruly mop of jet-black hair—was widely emulated. "The Hair" first appeared around 1982 with `Pornography` and peaked in "spiderweb" style around 1984, but its sudden disappearance in late 1986 when Smith got a military-style haircut provoked a swift and angry reaction from fans, reminiscent of the outrage when Elvis Presley cut his hair for the army in 1957. Smith subsequently learned his lesson and began growing it out again, with the iconic style returning to normal by 1992. "The day Robert Smith lost the hair, and angered cure fans around the world."

xref.title: Kurt Cobain Richest Dead Celebrity (Forbes 2006) – $50 Million, Beating Elvis, Lennon, and Morrison
xref.body: In October 2006, Forbes magazine published their annual list of the highest-earning dead celebrities, and Kurt Cobain topped the list at $50 million — ahead of Elvis Presley, John Lennon, and Jim Morrison. In 2006, Courtney Love sold a 25% stake in Nirvana's song catalogue to a New York licensing company called Primary Wave, which then had permission to license the songs for further commercial uses, generating additional revenue streams. "Kurt Cobain, richest dead celebrity on the planet."

xref.title: Claim to First Rock and Roll Record
xref.body: While the exact "first rock and roll record" is debated, "Rocket 88" by Jackie Brenston and his Delta Cats is strongly nominated, largely because producer Sam Phillips consistently touted it as such. Phillips' endorsement, coming from the discoverer of Elvis Presley, helped solidify this legend into a widely accepted fact. "It was because Sam Phillips said it was."

xref.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a queer Black woman from Cotton Plant, Arkansas, is widely called the "Godmother of rock and roll." She was a pioneering guitarist who transitioned to the electric guitar, revered by figures like Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Chuck Berry for her influential bridge between gospel blues and swing music. "A lot of people will point to sister Rosetta Thar, a guitarist who graduated to the electric guitar and has been called the Godmother of rock and roll."

xref.body: Bill Black, the bass player for Elvis Presley, initially harbored a strong dislike for the Fender Precision Bass. He reportedly struggled to master the instrument and found it difficult to play. xref.title: Legal and Financial Troubles
xref.body: Wes Scantlin, the leader of Puddle of Mudd, has a consistent history of legal and financial difficulties. These include multiple charges of domestic violence, a ban from Graceland after diving into Elvis Presley's swimming pool, and a charge of cocaine possession. He also faced arrest for vandalism after using a circular saw on a neighbor's patio and a sledgehammer on a brick wall following a dispute. The IRS pursued him for unpaid taxes, American Express for unpaid credit card bills, and his house was foreclosed by the bank due to overdue mortgage payments, after which he illegally returned to destroy property inside. "Wes Scotland, the leader of Puddle of Mud, seems to lose an unregular basis."

xref.title: London Calling Album Artwork
xref.body: The iconic artwork for "London Calling" features a black and white photograph with green and pink lettering, a color scheme that serves as a tribute to an old Elvis Presley record. The cover also famously depicts bassist Paul Simonon smashing his bass guitar, a moment captured at 10:50 PM on September 21, 1979, at the Palladium in New York City. This precise time is known because Paul's watch broke and stopped at the exact moment he destroyed his instrument. "First the color scheme, the black and white photo and the green and pink lettering. That's actually a tribute to an old Elvis Presley record."

xref.title: Musical Influences
xref.body: Growing up in a musical family, East Bay Ray was exposed to a wide range of influences, including instrumental surf rock. His heroes included Dick Dale, George Tomscow of The Fireballs, and Scotty Moore (who played in Elvis Presley's band) due to Moore's use of echo and reverb. Ray developed a distinctive guitar sound that was appealing to hardcore fans, a style heavily influenced by surf music. "He came from a musical family and was exposed to a lot of influences growing up, and that included instrumental surf rock."

xref.title: Pioneering Instrument Smashing
xref.body: In 1956, Rockin' Rocky Rockwell performed a "not-so-respectful" version of Elvis Presley's "Hound Dog" on "The Lawrence Welk Show." Upon finishing, he smashed his acoustic guitar to pieces, an act interpreted as commentary on the value of rock and roll music at the time and marking an early instance of instrument destruction. "That's when a guy named Rockin' Rocky Rockwell performed a not-so-respectful version of Elvis Presley's Hound Dog. And when he finished, he smashed his acoustic guitar to bits."
